key: ENERGY IS THE BIGGEST HEADLINE DRIVER, AND PUMP PRICES ARE REVERSING. Gasoline is the #1 contributor to 12-month headline CPI (+0.81 pp, just ahead of owners' equivalent rent at +0.77 pp) and PCE (+0.49 pp; +27.9% y/y), but it is falling at a ~31% annualized pace over the last 3 months in both indexes. Upstream energy is still up sharply on a 12-month basis (PPI diesel +78%, jet fuel +67%, finished consumer energy +21%), though those are also falling over 3 months. Airfares are NOT reversing (CPI +22% annualized over 3 months even as jet fuel fell ~31%).

PRICES IN ENERGY-EXPOSED SERVICES ARE RISING, BUT THE BASKET IS NARROW AND IT IS AIRFARES. Transport and delivery services are ~1.6-1.9% of core and add +0.27 pp to core CPI and +0.19 pp to core PCE; airfares (+23% CPI, +19.5% PCE) account for all of it (other transport items net slightly negative). Airfares dominate the energy-exposed transport basket; fuel costs are one possible explanation alongside demand and capacity (the data show rising prices, not causal pass-through). The rest of core runs ~2.1% y/y in CPI and ~2.9% y/y (2.2% annualized over 3 months) in PCE (weighted baskets, not official indexes). Freight PPI (+14%) and trade margins are pipeline risks. This does not explain why core PCE exceeds core CPI.

BEA'S SEPT 30 REVISION SHRANK THE CORE PCE-CPI GAP. Same-month comparison (July): 0.87 pp before the revision, 0.51 pp after; August: core PCE 3.01% vs core CPI 2.45% (0.56 pp). BEA's method changes cut measured portfolio-management inflation from 20.8% to 8.6% and software from 21.2% to 12.3% (July, y/y). Measured as excess over average core inflation, the two now add about +0.25 pp to core PCE (portfolio management ~0.10, software ~0.15; software is 1.2% of core PCE vs 0.04% of CPI): under half of the remaining gap, the rest unexplained here. The gap between core PCE and market-based core narrowed from +0.32 pp to +0.06 pp in July with the revision, and is ~0 in August (3.01 vs 3.03); the two indexes differ in scope and aggregation, so this gap is not the contribution of the excluded items. BEA Table 9.1U (headline only, Dec 2025-Aug 2026): PCE-only items +0.55 pp, shelter weight -0.46 pp.

AI PRICE PRESSURE IS VISIBLE UPSTREAM AND IN COMPUTERS, NOT ACROSS ELECTRONICS, AND THE DATA DON'T PROVE AI CAUSED IT. PPI electronic components +28% y/y and computers +22% (+75% annualized over 3 months); computers are +29% annualized over 3 months in both CPI and PCE (12-month: CPI +8.4%, PCE +8.4%). Against it: phones -14%, semiconductor-industry PPI -3%, hosting PPI +0.3%, application-software PPI -3.7%, and the CPI AI basket is -3.7% y/y. In the PCE AI basket (+10.5% y/y), software is 60% of the starting weight but ~90% of the 12-month contribution; software is +15.6% y/y but only +2.1% annualized over 3 months after BEA's revision.

UNDERLYING TREND IS NEAR 2.2-2.7%, AND MOMENTUM COOLED. Dallas trimmed-mean PCE 2.19% y/y (Aug), Cleveland trimmed-mean CPI 2.6%, Atlanta core sticky CPI 2.7% (2.4% annualized over 3 months). Core PCE annualized over 3 months: July 3.05% before the revision, 2.30% after, 2.05% in August, so part of the cooling is revision and part is new. Breadth (share of core PCE weight rising faster than 3% annualized over 3 months): July ~61% both before and after the revision (61.4% vs 60.3%), then 33% in August, a sharp one-month drop in new data, not a revision effect; core CPI 17%. On a 12-month basis 61% (PCE) vs 54% (CPI).

POLICY READ-THROUGH (interpretation, to test in Step 6): after BEA's revision core PCE is ~3.0% y/y but ~2.0% annualized over 3 months, and the asset-price measurement effect is much smaller (portfolio management now contributes ~0.15 pp to core PCE y/y as weight x rate, down from ~0.38; ~0.10 pp measured as excess over average core, as in the revision bullet above). What remains above target is concentrated: airfares (energy-exposed, not reversing), hospital services (+3.5% y/y, accelerating to +5.2% annualized), and housing (~3.1%), against an energy shock already reversing at the pump. None of this identifies causes or what another 25 bp hike would do.

index.CPI headline: Gasoline (+0.81 pp) and shelter (OER + rent +0.98 pp) dominate; gasoline now falling fast, so headline should ease.
index.CPI core: Shelter (~1.3 pp) plus airfares (+0.27 pp; energy-exposed, cause not established: fuel costs, demand and capacity are all possible); car and health insurance are the main drags. Core excluding transport/delivery runs ~2.1% (weighted basket).
index.PCE headline: Gasoline (+0.49 pp), owner housing (+0.36), hospitals (+0.18), airfares (+0.18) and software (+0.17) lead; drugs are the main drag.
index.PCE core: Owner housing (+0.40 pp), hospitals (+0.21, accelerating), airfares (+0.20), software (+0.19) and restaurant meals (+0.19). Financial fees fell out of the top 5 after BEA's method change (+0.19 pp, 6.6% y/y).
index.Market-based PCE headline: Excludes portfolio management and imputed bank services; gasoline, owner housing, hospitals, airfares and software lead. Contributions reconcile to BEA within 0.01 pp at 12 months.
index.Market-based PCE core: 3.03% vs core PCE 3.01%: after BEA's revision the gap between the two core rates has closed (July +0.32 -> +0.06 pp); the indexes differ in scope, so the gap is not a clean measure of the excluded items. Owner housing, hospitals, airfares, software and restaurant meals lead.
index.PPI final demand: Consumer services (33% weight, +3.8%) and energy (+21%) lead; trade margins on consumer goods (+5.3%, accelerating) add 0.7 pp, consistent with retailers/wholesalers widening margins rather than absorbing costs.
index.PPI intermediate: processed goods: Processed fuels (+26-33%) and durable manufacturing materials (+17%, e.g., metals) dominate; momentum easing.
index.PPI intermediate: unprocessed goods: Unprocessed nonfood materials EXCEPT fuel (53% weight, +28% y/y) account for nearly all of the 12.8% rise, but that series is falling at a -30% annualized pace over 3 months. Unprocessed fuel is down slightly y/y (-0.6% to -1.8%) and rising over 3 months. Cause of the non-fuel rise is not identified here (metals are a candidate to check).
index.PPI intermediate: services: Business services +2.9% (64% weight) plus freight transport (+9%) and trade margins (+10%): consistent with fuel costs passing through freight and distribution, though the data do not prove it.
index.PCE supercore (services ex energy & hous: Hospitals (+0.37 pp, accelerating), airfares (+0.35), restaurant meals (+0.34) and financial fees (+0.34, down from +0.72 before the revision). Excluding financial fees, supercore is ~3.31%.

CPI: Source: BLS CPI-U U.S. city average, Aug 2026; weights = BLS relative importance (Dec 2024/Dec 2025) updated by relative price change. 12m changes NSA; 3m annualized SA. Contributions are calculated (weight x change).
Note: CPI has no portfolio-management item, and software is only 0.03% of CPI, so the two biggest PCE-specific movers barely register here.
PPI: Source: BLS PPI FD-ID system, Aug 2026; weights = BLS relative importance (Dec 2025) within each parent basket. Named series use BLS commodity (WPU) or industry (PCU) indexes, NSA.
Trade services measure retailer/wholesaler margins; a rising trade index means margins are widening, not that goods prices rose.
PCE: Source: BEA NIUnderlyingDetail U20404/U20405, August 2026, post-Sept 30 2026 annual-update vintage (history revised Jan 2021 onward; new methods for portfolio management, software, legal services). Component set = Dallas Fed 178-component list (176 mapped); weights = nominal expenditure shares. SA only. Pre-revision version archived in Price indexes/archive/vintage_2026-09-27_pre_annual_update/.

Financial service charges, fees, and commissions (line 258) contains portfolio management and investment advice (line 268); see drill-down. Revision impact (12m, July): portfolio management 20.8% -> 8.6%; software 21.2% -> 12.3%; air transportation 16.8% -> 19.0%; owner-occupied housing 3.25% -> 3.22%.
Market-based PCE: Membership from BEA's official composition tables (market and other-than-market PCE categories, linked from BEA FAQ 83; 2009 vintage), mapped to current BEA lines by series code. Portfolio management and investment advice, mutual fund sales charges, trust services, financial services furnished without payment (lines 254-257), most insurance, gambling, net foreign travel and NPISH consumption are NON-market. Where BEA splits a leaf, its published market-only sub-lines are used (used autos line 14, used light trucks line 18, financial fees lines 259/261/264).

Checks (August 2026, post-revision): leaf spending matches every BEA market-based subcategory within $2 mn except line 218 (cable/streaming/AV services), missing from the Dallas component set (leaf total -0.92% vs BEA line 377). Summed contributions minus BEA published: headline +0.01 (12m), +0.07 (3m ann.); core -0.01, +0.08. A category-level version built only from BEA's published market-based subcategories reconciles within 0.013 pp (Market-based PCE/processed/category_components.csv). Rebuilt Sept 28 and rerun Oct 1 by Sonnet 5.5 subagents.
Trimmed & Sticky: Published data only (per Eli: no reconstruction). Cleveland and Dallas publish component tables (Dallas: 'Components included and excluded from this month's Trimmed Mean', with trim status color-coded); Atlanta publishes rates only. An earlier version of this sheet wrongly said Dallas publishes no component detail (corrected Oct 1 per audit).

Cleveland 16% trimmed-mean CPI 12-month rate cited elsewhere (2.57%, Aug 2026) is from Cleveland Fed's published chart data (mediancpi_chartdata.csv, column trimmedmeancpi), saved in inflation_data/raw/fed_expectations/.
Hypothesis analysis: Baskets are weight-averages of the component rates within core (calculated). Energy spillover = transport, travel and delivery services; AI-exposed = computers, software, phones/IT hardware, video equipment; Asset-price = financial services priced off asset values.
BEA Table 9.1U reconciles headline CPI and PCE monthly; summing Dec 2025-Aug 2026 gives the cumulative effects (PCE 2.60 vs CPI 2.90 over the period). BEA does not publish a core reconciliation.

Stress-test caveats: baskets and controls are weighted component averages, not official indexes; gross contributions are not a formal CPI-PCE decomposition; Table 9.1U monthly lines are rounded, so summed effects do not bridge exactly; none of these establish war or AI causation. PCE data are the post-Sept 30 2026 vintage; CPI/PPI are August 2026.
PCE supercore: Published (BEA NIPA Table 2.8.4 line 28, PCE services excluding energy and housing): 3.46% 12m, 2.33% 3m annualized, August 2026 (post-revision). Components = PCE services leaves (BEA U20404 line >= 150) excluding housing (lines 153-164) and electricity & gas (169-171); 77 components. Summed contributions: 3.48% 12m.

KEY FINDING (revised): financial fees now add +0.34 pp of the 3.48% (5.1% weight, +6.6% y/y; was +0.72 pp before BEA's method change). Excluding them supercore is ~3.31%; also excluding imputed bank services ~3.36%; also excluding air transportation ~3.02% (weighted component averages; calculated). Hospitals (+5.2% annualized over 3 months) are the item accelerating.

sources: CPI: BLS Public Data API (CUSR/CUUR0000 item series, 2017-2026) and BLS relative-importance tables Dec 2024 and Dec 2025 (Price indexes/CPI/raw/). 204 leaves; weights sum to 100.0%. Leaves without published indexes (unsampled items, legal, domestic services) have no data.
PPI: BLS API (WPS/WPU FD-ID series; WPU/PCU named series) and BLS PPI relative importance Dec 2025 (Price indexes/PPI/raw/).

PCE: BEA API NIUnderlyingDetail U20404 (prices) and U20405 (nominal spending), NIPA T20804/T20807, retrieved Oct 1, 2026 (post-Sept 30 annual update; latest = August 2026); Dallas Fed component list: 176 of 178 mapped (Price indexes/PCE/raw/). BEA Table 9.1U reconciliation (through Aug 2026) and NIPA Handbook ch. 5 (Table 5.B) PPI-source mapping (Price indexes/Cross-index analysis/raw/). Pre-revision outputs archived in Price indexes/archive/vintage_2026-09-27_pre_annual_update/.
Trimmed mean / sticky: Cleveland Fed median CPI component table; Dallas Fed trimmed mean PCE workbook; Atlanta Fed sticky-price CPI workbook (published values only).

Manager corrections: (1) PCE and market-based core use BEA's definition: exclude U20404 lines 73-103 (food & beverages off-premises), 113-119 (energy goods) and 169-171 (electricity & gas); clothing (104-112) and tobacco stay in core. An earlier version wrongly mixed food into core, and a later one wrongly dropped clothing; both are fixed. (2) 3-month contributions = weight x raw 3-month change, scaled to an annual rate at the aggregate level. (3) Tags corrected so 'less foods and energy' and 'less trade, transportation and warehousing' aggregates are not flagged.

Audit fixes (Codex audit 2026-09-27, applied 2026-09-28): market-based PCE rebuilt from BEA composition tables and verified against BEA subtotals; movers ranked by sign (upward = positive contributors only, downward = negative only; fewer than 5 shown when necessary); PPI unprocessed-goods finding corrected (the +28% series is nonfood materials EXCEPT fuel; cause not identified); wording fixes. Audit report: challenge research/working-notes/basket_audit1_2026-09-27.md.

Methods: contributions = start-of-period weight x component % change (3m uses annualized change). Direction: Accelerating if the 3m annualized rate is more than 1 pp above the 12m rate; Easing if more than 1 pp below. Excess vs 2018-19 = weight x (12m change minus the item's average 12m change in 2018-19). All contributions and basket aggregates are calculated, not published. Code: Price indexes/code/.
Stress test: independent critique by a second model (Sol) saved at challenge research/working-notes/basket_stress_test_sol_2026-09-27.md; material points are incorporated in the Summary.

Stress tests: v1 (Sol, Sept 27) and v2 (Sonnet 5.5, Oct 1) critiques in challenge research/working-notes/basket_stress_test_*.md. v2 corrections applied: same-month gap comparison; excess-over-core measure for portfolio management/software; revision vs new cooling separated; airfares not reversing; contrary AI evidence added.
